extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys and agents; USPTO practitioners; legal professionals involved in patent prosecution and disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: A USPTO Amended Final Order describing the legal standards, practitioner duties, micro-entity eligibility rules, and sanctions applicable where a practitioner presented erroneous Certifications of Micro Entity Status. It explains the regulatory requirements, the facts found, the rules violated, remedial actions, and factors considered in imposing discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'presenting any paper' to the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: A party, such as Respondent, presenting any paper to the USPTO (whether by signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating) certifies the statements set forth in 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The certification obligations attach whenever a practitioner signs, files, submits, or later advocates a paper before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification requirement — truthfulness and awareness of penalties (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(I))
rubrics_metrics.description: All statements made therein of the party's own knowledge are true, all statements made therein on information and belief are believed to be true, and all statements are made with the knowledge that whoever knowingly and willfully falsifies, conceals, or covers up a material fact, or knowingly and willfully makes any false, fictitious, or fraudulent statements or representations, shall be subject to the penalties set forth under 18 U.S.C. 1001 and any other applicable criminal statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False statements can trigger criminal penalties (18 U.S.C. 1001) and may jeopardize the probative value of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry requirement before presentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Certifications must be made 'to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must conduct a reasonable pre-filing inquiry under the circumstances before presenting certifications (failure to do so can constitute a rule violation).

rubrics_metrics.name: No improper purpose (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper is not being presented for any improper purpose, such as to harass someone or to cause unnecessary delay or needless increase in the cost of any proceeding before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper purposes include harassment, delay, or increasing costs; filings should be vetted to avoid such motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal contentions must be warranted or nonfrivolous (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The other legal contentions therein are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for the extension, modification, or reversal of existing law or the establishment of new law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorneys must ensure legal arguments are grounded in existing law or constitute a nonfrivolous attempt to change the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual allegations must have evidentiary support (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The allegations and other factual contentions have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, are likely to have evidentiary support after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual assertions should be backed by evidence or reasonably likely to be supported after further investigation; identify if contingent on future discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denials of factual contentions must be warranted (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: The denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence, or if specifically so identified, are reasonably based on a lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When denying factual allegations, practitioners must have evidentiary basis or reasonably state lack of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity eligibility — small entity requirement (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant qualifies as a small entity as defined in 37 C.F.R. § 1.27 without relying on a government use license exception under 37 C.F.R. § 1.27(a)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micro-entity status requires meeting small-entity criteria; do not rely on excluded exceptions when certifying micro-entity status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity eligibility — inventor/application count limit (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has been named as the inventor or a joint inventor on more than four previously filed patent applications, other than applications filed in another country, provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 111(b), or international applications for which the basic national fee under 35 U.S.C. 41(a) was not paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must check prior U.S. filings to ensure the inventor has not exceeded the four-application limit (subject to stated exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity eligibility — gross income limit (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor, in the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the applicable fee is being paid, had a gross income exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year, as most recently reported by the Bureau of the Census.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gross income is defined by IRC § 61(a); practitioners should verify income eligibility using the most recent Census median household income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity eligibility — assignment/license income limit (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has assigned, granted, or conveyed, nor is under an obligation by contract or law to assign, grant, or convey, a license or other ownership interest in the application concerned to an entity that, in the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the applicable fee is being paid, had a gross income exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for assignments/licenses to entities whose income would disqualify the applicant from micro-entity status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful false claim of micro entity status may constitute fraud (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(j); § 11.18(b)(I))
rubrics_metrics.description: A willful false claim of micro entity status may be considered fraud on the USPTO and can adversely affect the proceeding; referenced to criminal penalties (18 U.S.C. 1001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresenting micro-entity status, if willful, can lead to fraud findings and severe consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence in representing a client; failing to conduct reasonable inquiries under the circumstances or to have adequate procedures in place can violate § 11.103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes pre-filing inquiry and maintaining procedures (e.g., docketing) to ensure compliance with USPTO regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to integrity of the patent application process (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the integrity of the patent application process, including not conducting a reasonable pre-filing inquiry or lacking adequate procedures to ensure certifications complied with USPTO regulations, violates § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting erroneous certifications because of inadequate inquiry or systems can be characterized as prejudicial conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of firm procedures and docketing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms must have adequate procedures (such as docket management systems) to identify when micro-entity limits are exceeded and to ensure certifications comply with USPTO regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shortcomings in docketing or internal processes that prevent identification of disqualifying facts can contribute to practitioner liability; remediations (e.g., shared docket systems, internal audits) are relevant in mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to Notices of Payment Deficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: When the USPTO issues a Notice of Payment Deficiency (e.g., based on prima facie evidence that micro-entity limits were exceeded), the practitioner should change the entity status and pay the deficient amount or the application may be abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely correcting entity status and paying fees can mitigate consequences (failure to do so may lead to abandonment of the application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating and aggravating factors for sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors the OED Director considered in mitigation include: no prior professional discipline by the USPTO, acknowledgement of lapses and contrition, cooperation with OED's investigation (including offering interviews and providing supplemental responses), corrective actions taken prior to inquiry, and pro bono service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors can reduce the severity of imposed sanctions; conversely, the record may be used as an aggravating factor in future proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible sanctions and publication of disciplinary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions may include public reprimand; the OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at the OED's electronic FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the order; settlement can include waiver of rights and allocation of costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary outcomes may be publicly posted and cited in future matters; settlement terms can include explicit waivers (reconsideration, review, appeal) and each party bearing its own costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional authority for practitioner discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over the matter pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32 and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary proceedings proceed under these statutory and regulatory authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of post-settlement procedural rights
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the settlement, Respondent waived rights to seek reconsideration of the Final Order under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56, waived the right to have the Final Order reviewed under 37 C.F.R. § 11.57, and waived the right otherwise to appeal or challenge the Final Order in any manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement agreements in disciplinary matters commonly include waivers of administrative and appellate remedies as part of finality.
